question: In recent years, Disney has been asking high prices for its toys, which go children’s wish lists after they see Disney’s animated film characters.

The pricing policy adopted by the US multinational for its dolls is putting them beyond the means of many families who, given the massive promotional campaigns being run for animated films and the associated products for children, find themselves struggling to afford these toys given the high demand.

Besides the fact that children are finding it hard to get the dolls they want and this is a problem for parents, this matter also gives cause for concern over the protection of consumer rights and over whether European families can afford certain products. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
Will it investigate Disney’s pricing policy for its toys and assess whether this is in line with European competition and consumer protection laws?
What measures will it adopt to ensure that prices of Disney products are such that European households can afford these, without this compromising the company’s financial viability?
Is it conscious of the need to protect consumer rights and promote fair competition in the European market in this case?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.6.2024) The Commission is responsible for the enforcement of the EU competition rules established in Articles 101 and 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (‘TFEU’).

Article 101 TFEU prohibits agreements between two or more independent companies, which have as their object or effect the prevention, restriction or distortion of competition within the internal market. Article 102 TFEU prohibits companies that hold a dominant position within the internal market or in a substantial part of it from abusing that position.

Imposing unfair purchase or selling prices or other unfair trading conditions might amount to such an abuse. Currently, the Commission has no indication that the Walt Disney Company has concluded agreements that are contrary to Article 101 TFEU or that it holds a dominant position within the internal market and abuses its dominance contrary to Article 102 TFEU.

However, the Commission will carefully review any concrete information it receives that would point towards an infringement of the EU competition rules by the Walt Disney Company. Moreover, under EU consumer protection rules, traders selling goods to consumers have to ensure transparency about prices and must not engage in misleading commercial practices, nor directly exhort children to buy advertised products.

Member States have a primary responsibility to monitor the application of the relevant legal provisions and to take the necessary steps for enforcement. In its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission will continue monitoring the situation.
